text: Every day, your kidneys filter about 150 to 180 liters of fluid from your blood. That is enough to fill a bathtub. Yet you pass only about one to two liters of urine. So where does the rest go? Let's find out.

Your kidneys are two bean-shaped organs, each about the size of a fist. They sit just below the rib cage, one on each side of the spine. They are part of the urinary system, together with the ureters, the bladder and the urethra.
Blood reaches each kidney through the renal artery and leaves through the renal vein. At rest, the kidneys receive about a quarter of the blood your heart pumps, a little over a liter every minute.
Inside each kidney are about a million tiny filtering units called nephrons. Each nephron has a filter called the glomerulus, and a long tube called a tubule.
The glomerulus is a tangle of tiny blood vessels. Blood pressure pushes water, salts, sugar and waste out of the blood and into the tubule. Blood cells and large proteins stay behind.

Now the mystery. As the fluid flows along the tubule, the body takes back most of the water and the useful substances, like sugar and salts, into the blood. About ninety-nine percent of the filtered fluid is reabsorbed. Only the waste and the extra water are left as urine.
This lets your kidneys fine tune how much water and salt stay in your body, second by second.
The urine collects in the kidney, then travels down the ureters to the bladder. It leaves the body through the urethra.

The kidneys do more than clean blood. They release renin, which helps control blood pressure. They make erythropoietin, which tells your bone marrow to make red blood cells. And they help activate vitamin D.

Remember three things. The kidneys filter your blood. Most of the filtered fluid is taken back, and the rest becomes urine. And they also help control blood pressure and make red blood cells. If you have any concern about your kidneys, talk to a doctor. Next time, the immune system: your body's defense team.
